Hofstra enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a 22-10 overall record and a 12-6 Coastal Athletic Association record after finishing the regular season 21-10, 12-6 and then beating Towson 68-65 in overtime on March 9, 2026 and Monmouth 75-69 on March 10, 2026 to win the CAA automatic bid. Hofstra’s season profile is built on efficient perimeter scoring and sturdy half-court defense: through 25 games the Pride were scoring 76.6 points per game, allowing 68.0, shooting .447 from the field, .379 from three, and averaging 39.1 rebounds per game; by season end ESPN listed the team at 75.6 points, 39.3 rebounds, 12.8 assists, 44.2% shooting, and 36.8% from three over 34 games, showing a team that sustained its offensive identity across the full season. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/news/2026/3/4/mens-basketball-hofstra-wins-fourth-straight-downs-drexel-in-regular-season-finale.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Offensively, Hofstra is a traditional Claxton guard-led team that plays through its backcourt creators, especially Cruz Davis and freshman Preston Edmead. The statistical shape is clear: Davis finished as the lead scorer at 20.2 points and 4.6 assists per game, with 39.9% three-point shooting, while Edmead added 15.9 points and 4.4 assists on 38.3% from three. That two-guard creation shows up directly in named games. In the 78-67 road win at Towson on January 8, Davis exploded for 32 points and six rebounds. In the 66-62 win at Charleston on February 12, Davis had 23 points, six rebounds, and four assists. In the CAA title game against Monmouth on March 10, Edmead scored a season-high 26. In practical scouting terms, Hofstra’s offense is driven by high ball-screen creation, kick-out threes, and late-clock shotmaking from its guards; the evidence is the assist volume from Davis and Edmead, the team’s 241 made threes through 25 games, and repeated game recaps where one or both guards controlled closing possessions. A.J. Wills also functions as a situational spacer and late-clock shooter; against Monmouth on January 10, he opened overtime with a huge three, and the recap specifically noted he had also hit a big late three the previous game at Drexel. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2275/hofstra-pride))

Their frontcourt role players define the rest of the scheme. Biggie Patterson gives them a scoring forward who can finish and rebound; he had 20 points against Towson on February 7 and later posted 17 points and 10 rebounds against Stony Brook on February 28. Silas Sunday is the interior anchor rather than a featured post scorer, averaging 6.9 rebounds and 1.1 blocks while shooting 67.0% from the field. His value is in screen-setting, rim finishing, and defensive rebounding; on January 10 against Monmouth he had 11 rebounds, and Hofstra won despite shooting only 27.1% overall because it generated free throws and extra-possession offense. That is important context: this is not a beautiful motion offense, but it is a mature, possession-valuing group that can win ugly when the guards get downhill and the bigs clean the glass. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/news/2026/2/8/mens-basketball-pride-sends-message-with-rout-of-towson.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Defensively, Hofstra’s philosophy is to make games half-court and physical. Specific results support that more than any generic label would. They held Towson to 49 points on February 7 after leading 46-20 at halftime. They held Drexel to 51 points in the regular-season finale on March 3. They held Stony Brook to 29% shooting in a 67-58 win on February 28. Hofstra was also 16-1 when holding opponents under 70 points as of the February 21 win over Northeastern. The defensive tendency is clear: protect the paint with size, finish possessions with rebounds, and force opponents to operate deep into the clock rather than chase steals. Their steal rate is modest at 5.0 per game, but their rebounding margin and field-goal defense numbers show they prefer containment over gambling. The main vulnerability is against teams that can really shoot over the top; William & Mary’s 89-82 win on January 24 was explicitly attributed to Tribe hot shooting, and UNCW closed the final six points of a 70-66 win on February 14 when Hofstra could not get enough stops late. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/news/2026/2/8/mens-basketball-pride-sends-message-with-rout-of-towson.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Coaching philosophy under Speedy Claxton is visible in both style and season arc. Claxton earned his 100th career win on February 21, 2026, in an 82-68 victory at Northeastern, and the note that Hofstra is 31-10 under him in February points to a team that generally improves as the season goes along. His teams lean on veteran-style guard play, trust their primary creators in late-clock spots, and are comfortable in close games. His documented in-game adjustment history this season is strong. Against Drexel on January 3, Hofstra built an early 15-point halftime lead with a 16-6 run and then survived 70-67, showing tempo control after a hot start. Against Monmouth on January 10, Hofstra survived when regulation got away from it and then immediately scored via Wills’ overtime three, suggesting a prepared extra-session set. Against Towson on March 9 in the CAA semifinals, Hofstra stayed alive long enough for Edmead’s banked three with 0.3 seconds left in overtime to win 68-65. Against Drexel on March 3, the Pride trailed by 10 late in the first half, then used two Patterson baskets in the final minute before halftime to cut it to six and flipped the game after the break. Those are not abstract “adjustments”; they are concrete examples of Claxton teams re-centering through guard decision-making and defensive tightening. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/news/2026/2/21/mens-basketball-claxton-earns-100th-career-win-as-hofstra-tops-northeastern.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Clutch and late-game execution is one of Hofstra’s best selling points. On January 3, 2026, Hofstra beat Drexel 70-67 on the road. On January 10, 2026, Hofstra beat Monmouth 67-64 in overtime after Monmouth tied it with 50 seconds left; Hofstra never trailed in OT and went 4-for-4 at the line in the extra period. On February 12, 2026, Hofstra won at Charleston 66-62 in what the school called a “huge” road win. On March 9, 2026, Edmead hit the overtime game-winner with 0.3 seconds left to beat Towson 68-65. On the negative side, February 14, 2026 showed the risk profile: UNCW scored the final six points to beat Hofstra 70-66, and January 15, 2026 showed another late-game shortfall when Stony Brook beat the Pride 76-71 despite 22 points and eight rebounds from Edmead. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/news/2026/1/3/mens-basketball-pride-stays-hot-tops-drexel-for-sixth-consecutive-win.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Key players start with Davis, the primary closer and best all-around perimeter piece. He averaged 20.2 points and 4.6 assists, had 32 at Towson on January 8, 23 at Charleston on February 12, and 22 at Northeastern on February 21; he also reached 1,000 Hofstra career points in the Charleston win. Edmead is the breakout freshman and second primary creator: 15.9 points and 4.4 assists per game, 24 versus Monmouth on January 10, 22 at Stony Brook on January 15, 18 at William & Mary on January 24, a 19-point, seven-rebound game versus Drexel on March 3, the 0.3-second winner against Towson on March 9, and 26 in the title game against Monmouth on March 10. Patterson is the connective forward who gives them balance, with 20 against Towson on February 7 and 17 points, 10 rebounds against Stony Brook on February 28. Sunday supplies interior defense and rebounding, averaging 6.9 boards and 1.1 blocks while shooting 67.0%. German Plotnikov gives supplementary shooting and spacing; he scored 18 in the February 21 win at Northeastern. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2275/hofstra-pride))

Notable wins and losses sharpen the scouting picture. The best wins were Charleston by four on the road on February 12, Towson by 29 on February 7, Stony Brook by nine on February 28 while allowing 29% shooting, Towson by three in the CAA semifinals on March 9, and Monmouth by six in the CAA final on March 10. Those games revealed that Hofstra can win in multiple ways: perimeter shotmaking, defensive control, and one-possession composure. The revealing losses were Stony Brook 76-71 on January 15, William & Mary 89-82 on January 24, and UNCW 70-66 on February 14. Those losses showed the two recurring concerns: defending shot-makers for 40 minutes and generating enough half-court offense when late possessions become isolation-heavy. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/news/2026/2/13/mens-basketball-davis-tops-1-000-hofstra-points-lifts-pride-past-charleston.aspx?utm_source=openai))

As for Claxton’s NCAA Tournament history as a head coach, 2026 is his first actual NCAA Tournament appearance leading Hofstra. He also coached Hofstra to the 2020 CAA tournament title, but that NCAA Tournament was canceled, so there was no official round reached. Therefore his documented head-coaching NCAA tournament history is: 2026 - qualified; first appearance, rounds to be determined as of March 18, 2026; 2020 - earned berth via CAA title, tournament canceled before play. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/news/2026/3/10/mens-basketball-ticket-punched-hofstra-wins-caa-championship-over-monmouth.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Hofstra enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a classic mid-major auto-bid with a profile that is materially stronger in predictive metrics than in résumé metrics, but still short of true at-large caliber. As of Selection Sunday for the 2026 field, broad team-sheet aggregation sources list Hofstra at NET No. 88, KenPom No. 87, BPI No. 102, KPI No. 79, and Bart Torvik No. 91. Those same team-sheet sources also peg the Pride’s NET strength of schedule at No. 230 and nonconference NET SOS at No. 209, with an average opponent NET of 188. Hofstra is in the bracket as the CAA automatic qualifier at 24-10 and is listed as a No. 13 seed. ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/hofstra-pride))

The big-picture statistical identity is fairly clear. Hofstra outscored opponents 2571-2246 over 34 games, or 75.6 to 66.1 per game, with a +9.6 scoring margin. The raw shooting profile is strong: 44.2% from the field, 36.8% from three, and 74.6% at the line. Opponents shot just 38.7% overall and 31.6% from three. On the glass, Hofstra averaged 39.3 rebounds to opponents’ 33.8, a healthy +5.5 margin, while keeping turnovers to 10.6 per game. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Using the season totals from Hofstra’s official statistics page, the derived Four Factors are solid across the board. Hofstra’s effective field goal percentage computes to 52.2%, while opponents sit at 45.0%. Its estimated turnover percentage is 13.6%, which is comfortably low and consistent with a team that generally gets to its shots. Offensive rebounding rate comes out to 32.1%, and free-throw rate is 0.319 FTA per FGA. The three-point attempt rate is 43.7%, so this is meaningfully a perimeter-oriented offense: nearly 44% of Hofstra’s field-goal attempts come from beyond the arc. Those numbers depict an offense built on spacing, shot value, and ball security more than sheer interior volume. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

From the same season totals, Hofstra’s estimated raw offensive efficiency is about 110.2 points per 100 possessions, with raw defensive efficiency around 100.9, for a raw net efficiency of roughly +13.9. Estimated tempo is about 68.6 possessions per 40 minutes, which is moderately fast by mid-major standards but not extreme. Because adjusted efficiencies require opponent and venue adjustments, these are not KenPom-style adjusted numbers; still, they match the broader predictive profile: a good-but-not-elite team whose offense is the stronger unit and whose defense is capable enough to support it. A betting analysis citing KenPom-derived numbers shortly before the CAA tournament placed Hofstra No. 90 nationally in adjusted net rating at +8.4, which fits that same middle-band interpretation. ([predictem.com](https://www.predictem.com/college-basketball/william-mary-vs-hofstra-prediction-2026-03-08/?utm_source=openai))

The recent-form story is positive overall, though not linear. Hofstra had an obvious midseason wobble: a January 15 loss to Stony Brook despite hitting 14 threes, then a rough early-February stretch with losses to Northeastern, Towson, and Charleston, followed by a jarring 43-point outing in a 79-43 win over Hampton that illustrates how volatile their scoring distribution can be from game to game. But late February into March shows a team rounding into tournament shape. Hofstra beat Northeastern 82-68 on February 21, beat Stony Brook 67-58 on February 28, held Drexel to 51 points on March 3, crushed William & Mary 92-61 on March 8, and edged Towson 68-65 on March 9. The CAA tournament title run is the key signal: the William & Mary game showcased the offensive ceiling, while the Drexel and Towson games showed the half-court defense can carry them when the jumpers cool. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

That said, the exact “last 10 games” efficiency trend is only partially accessible from public sources. What is accessible points in a favorable direction. Team-sheet sources show Hofstra’s NET improving from a low of 120 on January 30 to 88 entering the tournament, evidence of a strong finishing kick. Another team-sheet source through March 10 gave Hofstra a 0-1 Quad 1 record, 2-2 in Quad 2, 10-4 in Quad 3, and 10-3 in Quad 4, which underscores that the résumé is built more on avoiding bad losses and winning the league than on collecting premium wins. In other words, the trend is upward even if the total body of work is not especially selection-committee proof absent the auto bid. ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/hofstra-pride))

Where the numbers diverge from conventional wisdom is in the balance between style and substance. A casual eye test might label Hofstra a pure jump-shooting mid-major because of the 43.7% three-point attempt rate and 36.8% three-point accuracy, and that is directionally true. But the deeper profile says they are not reckless. The turnover rate is low, the offensive rebounding is respectable at 32.1%, and the free-throw rate is not negligible. This is not just a boom-or-bust bomb-away team; it is a structurally competent offense that happens to prefer threes. Meanwhile, the defense may be a little better than the eye test suggests because opponents have been dragged down to 45.0% eFG and 31.6% from three over the full season. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Personnel usage supports that read. Cruz Davis led the team at 20.2 points per game, with Preston Edmead at 15.9, giving Hofstra two legitimate primary scorers. The rebounding is shared, led by Silas Sunday and Victory Onuetu at 6.9 boards per game apiece, which helps explain the team’s sturdier-than-expected offensive rebounding numbers. Hofstra therefore does not profile like a one-dimensional guard-only attack; it has enough frontcourt activity to survive poorer shooting nights. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Bottom line: Hofstra’s 2026 tournament profile is that of a dangerous No. 13 seed because the predictive systems see a top-90-ish team, not a fringe top-150 auto-bid. The résumé metrics are held down by a weak schedule, but the underlying numbers show real competence: strong shot quality and shot making, low turnovers, decent work on the offensive glass, a solid defensive shooting profile, and improving form entering March. If Hofstra springs an upset, it will likely be because the offense gets to its preferred high-volume three-point diet without sacrificing possession control. If it loses, the most likely explanation is that the schedule has masked a lack of high-end athletic margin and that the defense, while good statistically, is not disruptive enough to survive against a power-conference offense that wins the line and the glass. ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/hofstra-pride))
matchup-analyst:
Hofstra enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 24-10 after winning the CAA tournament, and the statistical profile is clear: this is a guard-led, jump-shot-capable team that still wins with physical rebounding and free-throw generation more than pure tempo. They averaged 75.6 points per game while allowing 66.1, shot 44.2% from the field, 36.8% from three, attempted 25.8 threes per game, and outrebounded opponents 39.3 to 33.8. Their offense is driven primarily by perimeter creators Cruz Davis, Preston Edmead, and German Plotnikov, while their frontcourt size with Silas Sunday (7'0", 282), Alex Tsynkevich (6'10", 245), Victory Onuetu (6'10", 235), and Joshua DeCady (6'8", 220) gives them a real second-chance and interior screen-setting backbone. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Style of play: Hofstra wants a half-court game where its guards can create advantages, spray out to shooters, and then cash in on foul-line possessions. The best evidence is their shot mix and game outcomes. On the season they made 322 threes in 34 games, nearly 9.5 per game, and in the CAA quarterfinal blowout of William & Mary they hit 14 threes while committing only 6 turnovers in a 92-61 win. Cruz Davis scored 30, German Plotnikov added 17, and Hofstra never trailed. When they can play from spacing and shotmaking, they become hard to guard. But the disruption points are specific: make them finish over length without fouling, shrink the floor against Davis/Edmead drives, and deny clean catch-and-shoot rhythm for Plotnikov. Charleston’s 66-64 win on January 29 is the clearest template: Hofstra shot just 33.3% overall, only 2-for-5 at the line, and despite 78 field-goal attempts scored only 64 points. Charleston forced volume without efficiency. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Press vulnerability: the season-long turnover number says Hofstra is not reckless, only 11.0 turnovers per game, but they are not a true pressure-proof backcourt either. They had 19 turnovers in the January 31 win at Monmouth, their season high, despite winning 73-57. Against William & Mary in the January 24 loss, Hofstra had only 8 turnovers, but William & Mary turned those into 11 points off turnovers while Hofstra got only 4, which shows that even moderate ball pressure can flip possession value if it creates live-ball mistakes. In the UNCW loss on February 14, Hofstra had 7 turnovers, but UNCW turned those into 12 points off turnovers and also won the paint 30-18, a sign that Hofstra’s guards can be sped up into bad floor balance even if the raw turnover total is not huge. The practical takeaway: use selective pressure after makes, trap the first side ball screen, and rotate to steal momentum rather than gambling every possession. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Zone vulnerability: the strongest available evidence is indirect but useful. Hofstra is much more comfortable when it can create off dribble attacks and kickouts than when it must repeatedly score over a loaded lane. Charleston held them to 26-for-78 shooting and only 2 free throws made in that January 29 game, exactly the kind of low-efficiency outcome that compact gap help or zone principles can produce. Towson’s CAA semifinal also mattered: Hofstra escaped 68-65 in overtime, but the game produced 0 fast-break points for either side, meaning Towson succeeded in forcing a static half-court grind. Hofstra survived because of shotmaking, not offensive flow. Against teams that flatten the pace and pack the elbows, Hofstra’s offense becomes more jumper-reliant. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Preferred pace and how to force the opposite: Hofstra is not an all-out transition team. Their recent tournament games show modest transition output: 8 fast-break points vs William & Mary in the quarterfinal, 0 vs Towson in the semifinal, and 18 allowed to Monmouth in the final while Hofstra still won with free throws and rebounding. In other words, they are comfortable in controlled games and do not need pace to score. To force the opposite, you need to make them defend early offense repeatedly and drag their big frontcourt into cross-matches. NC A&T nearly did this in a 79-78 Hofstra loss on January 22: Hofstra had 10 fast-break points, but NC A&T won the glass 45-30 and generated 20 second-chance points, making the game more athletic and less scripted. William & Mary also beat them 89-82 on January 24 by turning the game into a shot-volume shootout, scoring 18 threes and getting 38 bench points. The anti-Hofstra pace plan is not merely “run”; it is run selectively, attack before Sunday/Tsynkevich are set, and then keep the offensive rebounding pressure on so their half-court structure never stabilizes. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/boxscore.aspx?id=13846&path=mbball))

Size and athleticism mismatches by position: At point/lead guard, Preston Edmead is 6'1" and Cruz Davis is 6'3"; quick, downhill NCAA-caliber athletes can test them laterally. At the wing, Plotnikov is 6'5" and Biggie Patterson is 6'7", giving Hofstra good size, but neither profile suggests elite burst. Bigger slashers who can also defend physically are a problem because they disrupt Hofstra’s catch-and-shoot balance. At the 4/5, Hofstra has real mass: DeCady 6'8", Onuetu 6'10", Tsynkevich 6'10", Sunday 7'0". That helps on the glass, but it can be attacked in space. UNCW scored 30 paint points in a 70-66 win; NC A&T outrebounded Hofstra by 15; William & Mary’s January win featured 23 assists and 18 made threes, which implies Hofstra’s bigger lineups were stretched and rotated late. The mismatch to hunt is not post-up brute force; it is speed-to-space against their size, especially forcing Sunday or Tsynkevich into second-side closeouts. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/roster/_/id/2275/hofstra-pride?utm_source=openai))

Isolation vs. team offense tendencies: Hofstra’s exact Synergy possession-type percentages were not publicly retrievable from an accessible primary source, so I cannot honestly assign verified isolation-rate and team-offense percentages. What is verifiable is that their assist rate is moderate rather than elite: 343 assists on 886 made field goals, about 38.7% of makes assisted. In the most revealing wins and losses, that ratio swings with offensive comfort. In the 92-61 win over William & Mary, Hofstra had 12 assists and only 6 turnovers, and Davis also had 5 assists. In the January 24 loss to William & Mary, Hofstra had 11 assists on 28 makes, while William & Mary piled up 23 assists and 18 threes. That pattern strongly suggests Hofstra is best when guard creation bends the defense first and then the pass follows, rather than operating as a pure egalitarian movement offense. In scouting terms: they lean creator-led offense more than pure pass-chain offense, but I cannot give a sourced isolation percentage. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Transition offense and defense frequency: again, exact possession-frequency percentages were not available from an accessible primary source, so the cleanest sourced statement is game-level transition production. Hofstra had 10 fast-break points against NC A&T, 4 against William & Mary in the January 24 loss, 8 against William & Mary in the CAA quarterfinal, 0 against Towson in the semifinal, and in the CAA final allowed Monmouth 18 fast-break points while Hofstra won with free throws, rebounding, and late-shot execution. That is consistent with a team that can score in transition opportunistically but does not depend on it. Defensively, the concern is not transition volume every night; it is that when opponents do get them moving backward, their big lineups are less effective. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/boxscore.aspx?id=13846&path=mbball))

Coaching adaptability: Speedy Claxton’s staff does show evidence of game-to-game and in-event adjustment. Hofstra lost to William & Mary 89-82 on January 24, allowing 18 made threes and 23 assists; then in the CAA quarterfinal on March 8, Hofstra beat the same opponent 92-61, held them to 34.8% shooting and 22.7% from three, and cut its own turnovers to 6. That is the strongest available example of meaningful adjustment. There is also a Monmouth split: Hofstra won 67-64 in overtime on January 10 while shooting only 27.1% from the field, then beat Monmouth 73-57 on January 31 with a much cleaner 51.9% shooting night and finally beat them 75-69 in the CAA final by leaning on Edmead’s scoring and Sunday’s rebounding after Monmouth generated 18 fast-break points. That sequence suggests Claxton is willing to win different ways rather than insist on one script. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/boxscore.aspx?id=13847&path=mbball))

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must do five things. First, wall off Cruz Davis and Preston Edmead without overhelping to obvious kickout reads; Charleston’s 64-point containment game is the model. Second, play with selective pressure, not reckless gambling: make Hofstra initiate offense late and force their guards to start actions farther from the arc. Third, attack their big lineups in space before they can set the glass; UNCW, NC A&T, and William & Mary all showed versions of this. Fourth, finish possessions with gang rebounding, because Hofstra’s frontcourt size is real and gives them too many recovery chances if you leak out early. Fifth, offensively, hunt paint touch plus spray threes rather than static post-ups; William & Mary’s 18 made threes and 23 assists in the January 24 win is the cleanest offensive blueprint. Bottom line: if you let Hofstra play a clean half-court game with rhythm threes and foul-line control, they are dangerous. If you make them play late-clock, low-efficiency, multiple-effort possessions while dragging their size into space, they become very beatable. ([gohofstra.com](https://gohofstra.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))
